blurb: The EU AI Act, how the US, China and UK differ, the copyright fights, and rules that affect you.

cards.title: Regulating by risk

steps.p: Some uses are banned outright, such as social scoring and manipulative systems that exploit vulnerabilities.
AI used in hiring, credit, education, critical infrastructure and policing faces strict requirements for data, testing and human oversight.
Chatbots must disclose they are AI, and providers of general-purpose models have documentation and copyright obligations.

cards.aside: The Act entered into force in August 2024, with obligations phasing in over several years.

cards.q: Which practice does the EU AI Act ban outright?
cards.why: Social scoring. Rating people's trustworthiness from their behavior in ways that lead to unjustified or disproportionate treatment is in the prohibited category.

cards.statement: The EU AI Act applies only to companies based in the EU.
cards.why: False. Like GDPR, it applies to anyone placing AI systems on the EU market or whose AI outputs are used in the EU, wherever they are based.

cards.q: The maximum fine for using a banned AI practice under the EU AI Act is…
options: Up to €35 million or 7% of global annual turnover
cards.why: €35 million or 7% of worldwide turnover, whichever is higher — even steeper than GDPR's top tier.

cards.title: The EU's bans on prohibited AI practices took effect on February 2, 2025.
cards.detail: Obligations for general-purpose AI model providers followed on August 2, 2025, with most high-risk rules scheduled for later years.

cards.statement: Under the EU AI Act, chatbots must make clear to people that they are interacting with an AI.
cards.why: True. This transparency duty covers systems interacting with people, along with labeling certain AI-generated content such as deepfakes.

cards.title: Different philosophies

steps.p: No comprehensive federal AI law. Policy shifts with presidential executive orders, while states like Colorado and California pass their own rules.
Specific rules for algorithms, deepfakes and generative AI, including registration and requirements on content.
A lighter, sector-led approach, plus a government institute that tests frontier models.

cards.aside: Companies operating globally must satisfy all of these at once.

cards.q: What happened to President Biden's 2023 executive order on AI?
cards.why: Revoked by President Trump on his first day back in office, replaced by orders emphasizing US AI leadership and reduced regulation.

cards.statement: China requires providers of public generative AI services to follow rules on content and to file with regulators.
cards.why: True. Its 2023 interim measures on generative AI require registration, security assessments and content consistent with official values.

cards.q: In February 2025, the UK's AI Safety Institute was renamed the…
cards.why: AI Security Institute, signaling a focus on national security risks such as cyber and chemical or biological misuse.

cards.title: California's governor vetoed a major frontier AI safety bill in 2024, then signed a narrower one in 2025.
cards.detail: SB 1047, which would have imposed liability-linked safety duties, was vetoed. SB 53, signed in September 2025, instead requires large frontier developers to publish safety frameworks and report serious incidents.

cards.statement: A single global treaty binds every country to the same AI rules.
cards.why: False. There are international agreements, such as the Council of Europe's 2024 AI convention, but they cover only signatories. Rules differ greatly by country.

cards.title: The training data fight

steps.p: Is training an AI on copyrighted books, articles and images without permission legal? In the US, it hinges largely on "fair use".
Authors, newspapers, artists, record labels and stock photo companies have sued AI developers.
Courts have begun to split the issue: how data was obtained, and whether outputs compete with the originals, both matter.

cards.aside: Outcomes will shape how future models are built and who gets paid.

cards.q: In 2025, a US judge in the Bartz v. Anthropic case ruled that…
options: Training on lawfully acquired books was fair use, but keeping pirated copies was not
cards.why: A split ruling. Training itself was found transformative, but downloading pirated books was not excused. Anthropic later agreed to a settlement of about $1.5 billion.

cards.statement: In the US, a work generated entirely by AI with no human authorship cannot be copyrighted.
cards.why: True. The Copyright Office requires human authorship, and a federal appeals court upheld that in 2025. Human selection and arrangement of AI output can still be protected.

cards.q: Which US fair-use factor asks whether AI outputs substitute for the original works?
options: The effect on the market for the original
cards.why: Market effect. If AI outputs compete with and replace the originals, this factor weighs against fair use — a central argument in news publishers' lawsuits.

cards.title: The New York Times sued OpenAI and Microsoft in December 2023 over the use of its articles in training.
cards.detail: It alleged millions of articles were used without permission and showed examples of models reproducing passages nearly word for word. The companies argued training is fair use.

cards.statement: A 2025 US ruling found that a company's use of Westlaw legal summaries to train an AI tool was not fair use.
cards.why: True. In Thomson Reuters v. Ross Intelligence, the court found the copying was not transformative, partly because Ross built a competing product. The AI involved was not generative.

cards.title: Privacy, fairness and deepfakes

steps.p: Data protection laws like GDPR apply to personal data used in AI systems, including in training.
Some places require audits of AI used in hiring and lending, after high-profile cases of biased systems.
New laws target non-consensual intimate deepfakes and require platforms to remove them.

cards.aside: These are the AI rules most likely to touch your own life.

cards.q: Why did Italy's data protection authority temporarily block ChatGPT in 2023?
options: Concerns about personal data processing and age verification
cards.why: Privacy. The regulator cited the lack of a legal basis for training on personal data and no age checks. Access returned after OpenAI made changes.

cards.statement: Amazon scrapped an experimental AI recruiting tool after it learned to penalize résumés that mentioned the word "women's".
cards.why: True, Reuters reported in 2018. Trained on a decade of mostly male hires, it learned to downgrade signals associated with women.

cards.q: New York City's Local Law 144 requires employers using automated hiring tools to…
options: Commission an annual bias audit and notify candidates
cards.why: Bias audits and notice. In force since 2023, it was one of the first laws specifically targeting AI in hiring.

cards.title: The US TAKE IT DOWN Act, signed in 2025, criminalizes publishing non-consensual intimate images — including AI deepfakes.
cards.detail: It also requires platforms to remove such content within 48 hours of a valid request from the person depicted.

cards.title: Know your workplace's AI rules
cards.body: Most organizations now have policies on what can be pasted into AI tools. Leaking customer data or confidential code into the wrong tool is a common, avoidable mistake.
cards.challenge: Find your workplace or school's AI policy and check what data you're allowed to share with which tools.
